title: ‘I Is Another’ Trailer: Claes Bang Stars As Heinrich Himmler’s Double-Dealing Massage Therapist In Locarno-Bound Drama
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie First Look At Josh Henderson In Cold Case Thriller ‘Bulldogs’ As Filming Gets Underway In L.A. Demían Bichir & Danny Ramirez Join U.S.-Mexico Border Doc ‘Desert Angel’ As Executive Producers Gavin Leatherwood Joins ‘It Happened One Summer’ As Filming Gets Underway In New York View All August 4, 2026 4:20am EXCLUSIVE: Felix Randau’s post-World War Two drama I Is Another , starring Claes Bang as Heinrich Himmler’s controversial massage therapist Felix Kersten, world premieres at the Locarno Film Festival this week and Deadline can reveal the trailer. The historical drama delves into the conflicting accounts around Kersten’s conduct during World War Two. The late physiotherapist claimed he used his relationship with Himmler to save the lives of 60,000 Jewish people in the final days of the war and also claimed he had used his influence to help stop a plan to deport the entire Dutch population to Eastern Europe. Hit 'Four Minus Three' His accounts have been challenged since and mystery still swirls around the truth of what really happened. Watch on Deadline Randau delves into Kersten’s story through an imagined 1952 train trip from Germany to Oslo, where the therapist was hoping to receive the Nobel Prize. On route, he is accosted by journalist Hedda (Valerie Pachner) who demands a one-on-one interview with Kersten, during which she presents evidence suggesting he was far from being on the right side of history. A psychological game of cat and mouse ensues. Randau was last in Locarno with his 2017 film Iceman about the fight for survival of a Neolithic clan in the Ötztal Alps more than 5,300 years ago. I Is Another is produced by Ostlicht Filmproduktion (Marcel Lenz, Claritta Kratochwil) in co-production with WEGA Film (Veit Heiduschka, Christian Bachmann, Julia Heiduschka), in collaboration with Mitteldeutscher Rundfunk, BR, and Arte. title: Spotify Hits Milestone of 300 Million Premium Subscribers
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 4, 2026 4:15am Photo Illustration by Chris McGrath/Getty Images Audio streaming giant Spotify posted a second-quarter revenue gain and ended June with 300 million paying premium subscribers, up from 293 million as of the end of March and slightly above the forecast 299 million, “reflecting … year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter growth across all regions.” The company described this as “a milestone no audio streaming service has ever reached.” Monthly active users (MAUs) grew to 777 million, slightly below the projected 778 million, from 761 million in the previous quarter. Revenue growth for the quarter accelerated to come in at 14 percent, or 15 percent on a constant currency basis, to get the company to €4.8 billion ($5.5 billion), in line with its forecast. Operating income hit €655 million ($754 million) in the second quarter, exceeding management guidance and up 61 percent from the year-ago period despite a 3 percent increase in operating expenses, “driven by temporary investments in marketing and cloud/AI spend.” Related Stories Music Vicki Wickham, Influential 'Ready, Steady, Go!' Talent Booker and Producer, Dies at 87 Movies 'The Green Eyes,' Inspired by Resignation Syndrome, Opens Locarno With a Story Told From a Refugee Child's Perspective to "Try to Revive Empathy" Profitability has been in the investor spotlight after price increases and cost cuts. Spotify shares dropped more than 4 percent in pre-market trading. “We have a scale that few companies in history have reached, a business that is healthy and compounding, and opportunities only we are positioned to pursue,” said co-CEO Alex Norström. “Spotify lives across your whole day — the commute, the workout, studying, gaming, the dinner table, and sleep. At our scale, that is rare… Our position gives us an opportunity space as wide as our users want it to be.” Added co-CEO Gustav Söderström: “Investor Day described where we believe Spotify is going in the future. This quarter demonstrated that we are already building that future: better engineering, faster shipping, new products and new ways for users to engage. We are still in the very early stages of what is possible and will continue to have a high bar for investments.” He concluded: “Our job remains the same: understand the technology early and deeply, and turn it into something people love. Creating value for our stakeholders.” For the third quarter, Spotify predicted 305 million premium subs and 788 million MAUs, as well as operating income of €​670 million and revenue of €​5 billion. “Our business performed well in the second quarter, led by strength in subscribers and profitability,” Spotify said. “Overall, we view the business as well positioned to deliver improved growth and margins in 2026 as we reinvest to support our long-term potential.” THR

title: David Ellison Says Opposition to Paramount-Warner Bros. Is Over His Control of CNN, Claims He Will Not ‘Bend Newsrooms to My Views’
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 4:02am PT David Ellison Says Opposition to Paramount-Warner Bros. Is Over His Control of CNN, Claims He Will Not ‘Bend Newsrooms to My Views’ By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest David Ellison Says Opposition to Paramount-Warner Bros. Is Over His Control of CNN, Claims He Will Not ‘Bend Newsrooms to My Views’ 26 minutes ago Spotify Notches 300 Million Premium Subscribers 1 hour ago Sony Pictures Revenue Drops 13% in June Quarter, Music Segment Sales Jump 21% 4 days ago See All Getty Images; CNN Paramount CEO David Ellison said he believes the antitrust litigation filed by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America isn’t about market share but about “whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN .” Ellison, in an op-ed published by the New York Times Tuesday, noted, “There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions.” He reiterated his pledge that CNN would remain independent under a merged Paramount- Warner Bros. Discovery and that its journalists “will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause.” Related Stories David Ellison Addresses Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Delay Amid State AGs' Lawsuit in Staff Memo: 'The Facts and the Law Are on Our Side' How Strong Is the Democratic State AGs' Lawsuit Aiming to Block Paramount's Warner Bros. Takeover? “Unfortunately, I can’t give anyone a view into my heart and mind, but I can share this: I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans; and when it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. Popular on Variety The Paramount chief continued, “Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause. These were founding principles for both CNN and CBS News, for legends like Ted Turner and Edward R. Murrow, and it is exactly that kind of independence that has always fueled the greatness of ‘60 Minutes.’” Ellison said he has not heretofore publicly weighed in on the litigation aimed at blocking the Paramount-WBD merger because “I believe that anyone who oversees a news organization — I am chief executive of Paramount, which owns CBS — shouldn’t put a finger on the scale, especially on matters involving his own company.” So “when California’s attorney general, 11 other state attorneys general and, a day later, the Writers Guild of America sued to stop the deal, I stayed quiet. I quickly learned such restraint has costs. While I was silent, others were happy to write my story for me. No more.” In the new business, Ellison wrote, “There is much ground to recover.” He cited the latest polling from Gallup that found 28% percent of Americans “trust the news — the lowest ever recorded.” “The temptation is to say the problem lies elsewhere. Our obligation is to look inward and say: We can do better. We are in a moment when Americans trust few institutions, but journalists haven’t always helped their case by refusing to engage with critiques,” Ellison wrote. Ellison had hoped to have closed Paramount’s $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery by now. Instead, he’s facing a protracted legal fight that threatens to push the consummation of the merger into 2027 — or derail it altogether. The 12-state coalition alleges a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. will unlawfully reduce competition in the basic cable and theatrical distribution markets. The WGA’s lawsuit argues that it will also harm the marketplace for writers. Last Friday, Paramount Skydance asked a judge to schedule its upcoming antitrust trial beginning Nov. 4, 2026 , while the states and the WGA asked for the trial to commence April 5, 2027. The parties are awaiting the judge’s ruling on the trial date. There’s been speculation that the states might drop their suit if Paramount agreed to spin off CNN. But California attorney general Rob Bonta, who is leading the state AGs’ lawsuit to block the merger, has denied this. “Spinning off one channel from a media conglomerate is not a sufficient remedy to protect consumers and preserve competition in the film and television industry,” Bonta said in a July 15 post on X. Separately, last month a Paramount shareholder sued David Ellison and his tech billionaire father Larry Ellison, alleging they cut an “illegal” deal with President Donald Trump to secure U.S. governmental approval for the takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. In return, according to the lawsuit, the Ellisons offered “the opportunity to improperly funnel cash” to the president by settling his legal claims against CNN, and they allegedly promised that CNN anchors whom Trump does not like would be fired after the WBD takeover. In response, a Paramount spokesperson said in part, “This lawsuit recycles allegations that have already been reported and already addressed. As we’ve said consistently: no commitments from either David or Larry Ellison have been made to any government body, State AG, or federal agency regarding the future of CNN or any other news property, other than the goal to deliver truth-based journalism.” Ellison, in the NYT op-ed, said the lawsuits filed by the states and the WGA “imagine a Hollywood that no longer exists — an industry ruled by a handful of legacy studios.” Echoing points Paramount has made previously, Ellison said that if you add up every hour Americans spend watching TV, a combined Paramount-Warner would account for less than 20% of all watch time — “competing every day against Netflix, Amazon, Apple, which are all companies whose resources dwarf ours.” If you add in viewing of YouTube’s user-generated content, Paramount-WBD’s share would be around 13%. He said a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. would account for just 18% of the domestic box office over the past 12 months and only 22% on average over the past two years. “Those are not the numbers of a company that can dictate what audiences watch or what writers get paid,” Ellison wrote. That’s why “I believe this fight is not really about market share,” but about control of CNN, Ellison said. If it were about Paramount-WBD’s market power, he argued, “it wouldn’t have been reviewed or approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States, the European Union and China.” A combined Paramount-Warner Bros., Ellison wrote, will reinvigorate the entertainment industry. “Hollywood is losing ground to technology platforms whose algorithms reward the loudest voices. The work is leaving, especially from California — where I grew up and where I’m raising my family — draining the deepest pool of creative talent ever assembled,” he wrote in the Times op-end. Ellison also called out “commitments we have made for the proposed Paramount-Warner,” to release 30 theatrical films a year; 170 television series annually, “for our own platforms and for our competitors’”; and more than $30 billion in annual content investment. “I understand that promises from an executive in the middle of a merger invite skepticism. So judge us by the year we just had,” the exec wrote. “Since I took over Paramount, we have nearly doubled our theatrical slate from eight films last year to 15 and greenlit 40 new or returning series for Paramount+, our streaming service. You can expect 90 series from our television studios in 2026. We raised our content investment by $1.5 billion. We did that before the deal was signed and any lawsuit was filed, because making more is the whole point of the company we are building.” Ellison concluded his op-end with this: “Hollywood’s story can have a happy ending only when we connect with our audience. It’s the audience — the American people — who have the final say in whether a movie succeeds or fails, whether a news organization thrives or withers and therefore whether our industry succeeds or fails. I want to build a company with the strength and resources to deliver for those audiences who turn to us, for the storytellers who rely on us and for the country that dreamed this all up.” Netflix Inks Exclusive Deal for Video Episodes of Vox Media Podcasts ‘Unexplainable,’ ‘Switched on Pop’ About 300 Netflix Titles Used Generative AI This Year, Company Reveals Netflix Among Parties in Early Talks to Buy Letterboxd: Report LISTEN: Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Fight in France Over Streaming Quotas and Theatrical Windowing Rules Chloe Fineman Among Four Cast in ‘Myron Bolitar’ Series at Netflix Netflix Orders ‘Monopoly’ Competition Series With $2 Million Dollar Prize Loading comments... title: Jesse Eisenberg Musical ‘The Debut’ Set to Close London Film Festival
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 4:00am Julianne Moore in 'The Debut' Courtesy of Lionsgate Jesse Eisenberg ‘s latest film, musical comedy-drama The Debut , is set to close the 70th BFI London Film Festival . The Oct. 18 closing night gala will be the U.K. premiere of the movie, with its writer-director expected to attend alongside his cast members. Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Havana Rose Liu, Bernadette Peters, Colton Ryan, Lilli Cooper, Maulik Pancholy and Bonnie Milligan join Eisenberg in The Debut , following a shy woman (Moore) who is unexpectedly cast in a local production of an original musical. Under the spell of the strong-willed and enigmatic director (Giamatti), she loses herself in the role and the high-stakes world of this community theatre production. Related Stories Movies Cabo Verde Looks Beyond the World Cup, Ivory Coast Gets Animated, Zimbabwe Has Ambition: A Chat With Locarno Open Doors Film Producers TV Disney+ Sets Release Date for Season 2 of Hit Thriller Series 'Made in Korea' Eisenberg returns to the London Film Festival following the premiere of A Real Pain in 2024, which nabbed him an Oscar nomination for best original screenplay. “I am both honored and honoured to be bringing The Debut to the 70th BFI London Film Festival,” joked Eisenberg about the U.S.-U.K. spelling. “What a wonderful thrill to be the closing night gala, and I can’t wait to share the incredible performances by the cast with a London audience.” Kristy Matheson, artistic director of the BFI London Film Festival, added: “We are thrilled to welcome writer-director Jesse Eisenberg back to the LFF to close the 70th edition of the festival with his deliriously funny and heartfelt film, The Debut . With its knockout performances and brilliantly sharp script, we’re excited to share this film, which will have audiences in its thrall and renewed by the joyous and soulful power of cinema.” Last week, it was confirmed that this year’s BFI London Film Festival will open with the Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman-starring Elsinore , based on the life of late actor Ian Charleson. The 70th instalment runs from Oct. 7-18. Lionsgate will release The Debut in U.K. cinemas on Jan. 15, 2027. THR

title: Spotify Notches 300 Million Premium Subscribers
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 3:01am PT Spotify Notches 300 Million Premium Subscribers Music streamer's Q2 2026 subscription revenue increases 15% and ad revenue ticks up 1% By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest David Ellison Says Opposition to Paramount-Warner Bros. Is Over His Control of CNN, Claims He Will Not ‘Bend Newsrooms to My Views’ 15 minutes ago Sony Pictures Revenue Drops 13% in June Quarter, Music Segment Sales Jump 21% 4 days ago Disney Expected to Sell 50% Stake in A+E to Hearst for More Than $1 Billion 5 days ago See All Getty Images Spotify ‘s Premium customers grew to 300 million in the second quarter of 2026, after the music streamer gained 7 million paying subscribers, exceeding its previous guidance. Total monthly active users, including those on the free, ad-supported tier, stood at 777 million as of the end of Q2. That slightly undershot previous guidance of 778 million, which the company attributed to ongoing “product optimizations” in the quarter. Related Stories David and Larry Ellison Sued by Paramount Investor Alleging 'Illegal' Side Deal With Donald Trump to Secure U.S. Approval for Warner Bros. Takeover Warner Bros. Discovery Sues Amazon, Accusing It of 'Lawless Employee Shopping Spree' Including Poaching HBO Veteran Pia Barlow For Q2, the company reported revenue of €4.78 billion, up 14% and in line with its forecast. Operating income came in at €655 million and gross margin hit an all-time high of 33.4% (above previous guidance of €630 million and 33.1%, respectively). Net income was €545 million, compared with a net loss of -€86 million in the year-ago period. Popular on Variety Subscription revenue in the quarter grew 15% to €4.33 billion, while ad revenue inched up 1% to €446 million. Spotify said the improvement in gross margin in Q2 was driven by Premium gains (as revenue growth outpaced music costs net of marketplace programs, audiobooks costs and video podcast costs). On the ad-supported side, gains were driven by “favorable podcast and tax impacts, which more than offset music costs” and other costs of revenue. For Q3, Spotify expects revenue of €5.0 billion, operating income of €670 million and gross margin of 32.9%. It projects Premium subscribers of 305 million and total monthly active users of 788 million (implying the addition of approximately 11 million net new MAUs in the quarter). Spotify called out the launch of new initiatives in Q2 including Reserved in the U.S., which gives an artist’s most dedicated fans exclusive early access to concert tickets, and Personal Podcasts, letting users generate personalized AI-powered audio episodes. On Tuesday alongside the Q2 earnings results, Spotify announced a new agreement with Merlin for Spotify’s upcoming fan-made covers and remixing tool, which gives artists on labels under Merlin’s Spotify agreement the option to participate. As previously announced, Spotify’s tool will launch as a paid add-on, which “will create an additional revenue stream for participating artists,” the streamer said. Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström said in announcing the results, “We have a scale that few companies in history have reached, a business that is healthy and compounding, and opportunities only we are positioned to pursue. Spotify lives across your whole day — the commute, the workout, studying, gaming, the dinner table, and sleep. At our scale, that is rare… Our position gives us an opportunity space as wide as our users want it to be.” Co-CEO Gustav Söderström added, “This quarter demonstrated that we are already building that future: better engineering, faster shipping, new products and new ways for users to engage. We are still in the very early stages of what is possible and will continue to have a high bar for investments… Our job remains the same: understand the technology early and deeply, and turn it into something people love. title: ‘Gagarine’ Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh Talk ‘The Green Eyes’ as Kinology Announces First Sales: ‘Dreamers Know No Borders’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 2:45am PT ‘Gagarine’ Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh Talk ‘The Green Eyes’ as Kinology Announces First Sales: ‘Dreamers Know No Borders’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘Gagarine’ Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh Talk ‘The Green Eyes’ as Kinology Announces First Sales: ‘Dreamers Know No Borders’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Locarno’s First Look Section Reveals Six Uruguayan Titles, From Family Stories to Drama About Desire That ‘Persists Across Oceans’ 3 weeks ago See All 'The Green Eyes' 2026 June Films – Haut et Court – Les Films du Fleuve - Hobab – France 3 Cinéma Having boarded as the sales agent of Locarno Film Festival ‘s “ The Green Eyes ,” Kinology has pre-sold “The Green Eyes” to Benelux (Cinart), Switzerland (Filmcoopi), Turkey (Chantier) and the former Yugoslavia region (MCF). Distribution in France will be handled by Haut et Court, one of the film’s producers. Directed by Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh – also known for “ Gagarine ” – the film will open this year’s Locarno’s Film Festival on Aug. 5, playing at Locarano’s Piazza Grande. Related Stories 'Matchbox' Trailer: John Cena Stars in Toy Car Action Movie From Apple TV James Gunn Gave ‘Big Brother 28’ Star Rick Devens a Cameo in ‘Man of Tomorrow’ but He ‘Had to Cancel’ “Fanny and Jérémy are among the most inspired and inspiring French filmmakers today, and Kinology couldn’t be happier to be part of their magnificent comeback after the wonderful ‘Gagarine’,” said its founder and CEO Grégoire Melin, noting their “unique blend of social and magical realism.” Popular on Variety The film is produced by June Films and Haut et Court and co-produced by Les Films du Fleuve and Hobab. In “The Green Eyes,” Liatard and Trouilh follow little Chaya, who lives with her family in the Landes region in France. But when they learn they’re being evicted, her older brother Nour falls into a mysterious sleep. “We first learned about ‘resignation syndrome’ five years ago, through a photography exhibition featuring two sisters affected by this condition,” Liatard and Trouilh told Variety . “These little girls were sleeping side by side, locked in a deep sleep ever since their family’s request for asylum had been denied. Those images deeply moved us. When we realized that hundreds of children had been affected by this condition, we wondered what these young children, trapped in their sleep, were dreaming about. That was the starting point for our desire to tell a story from a child’s perspective and dive into the dreams of a little girl who will do everything she can to wake her big brother up.” Liatard and Trouilh decided to answer Variety ’s questions together. “We do everything together,” they admitted. “We’ve been working as a directing duo for over 10 years now, and we feel lucky to be able to share this journey together. We still don’t divide up the work.” Thorough research was important in order to address this disease in the film. “It truly exists, even if we then venture into the realms of fiction and magic. We met doctors who specialize in this disease and young people who have awakened from it, sometimes after several years of deep lethargy. These powerful testimonies conveyed to us the sheer strength of these children.” They also inspired the resilience of Chaya and Nour’s. “In our story, Chaya never loses hope of saving her brother, and it is thanks to the love that binds them and the power of her imagination that she succeeds.” Douae Butarbuch M’Zaouki, Sayyid El Alami, Anamaria Vartolomei, Arcadi Radeff, Omar Al Jbaai star. Liatard and Trouilh combined reality and fiction in their award-winning “Gagarine,” where a boy who wants to become an astronaut tries to save his home from demolition. “We love to explore reality without being realistic! Diving into the imagination and our characters’ dreams allows us to explore their emotions in a very visual way.” In “The Green Eyes,” the Landes forest, where they filmed, is already “magical in itself.” “There’s this lighthouse standing in the middle of the pine forest, and a little village covered in sand. It’s a paradise for these children, but also the place where all their traumas are replayed,” they said. They also praised Guillaume Laurant (“Amélie,” “I Lost My Body”), who joined them as a screenwriter. “He shared some of the magic of his vision with us.” “It’s always a major challenge for us to strike the right balance between realism and magical elements. On the one hand, it was important to ground the film in real everyday life, and the archive footage helps us connect with the reality of the syndrome. On the other hand, we wanted to delve into Chaya’s imagination until the boundary between dream and reality gradually blurred.” They enjoy focusing on younger protagonists who are not afraid to dream. “Dreamers know no borders; they invent the worlds of their choice. These worlds are refugees, and when reality becomes too violent, they can serve as escape routes,” they noted. “It’s true that children and teenagers often find it easier to immerse themselves in their imaginations. title: Mary Rivera, Ned’s Grandma in ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home,’ Dies at 82
full_text: Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 2:42am Mary Rivera Sony Pictures Mary Rivera, the Filipina actress who played Ned’s grandma (or lola) in Spider-Man: No Way Home , has died. She was 82. She died April 15 in Honolulu, Hawaii. TMZ reported that Rivera had suffered a stroke before her death. Rivera was born in Iloilo Province, in the Philippines on June 2, 1943. She attended the University of San Agustin in Iloilo City and graduated in 1964 with a degree in education. After college she worked for the radio station Kanlaon Broadcasting System. It it unclear when she moved to U.S., but she lived in Hawaii before her death and had worked as a teacher and was a retired church missionary. Related Stories Music Vicki Wickham, Influential 'Ready, Steady, Go!' Talent Booker and Producer, Dies at 87 TV Scott Hylands, Star of TV's 'Night Heat' on Both Sides of the Border, Dies at 83 A non-professional actor, Rivera won the part of Ned’s lola after sending an audition tape to producers of No Way Home , who had placed an ad on Facebook looking for a Filipina performer aged 50-90. In an interview with the Philippines’ Star FM Baguo , Rivera said that her daughter Angela Kelly had seen the Facebook ad and urged her to audition. Rivera said that she had quoted lines from The Grapes of Wrath in her audition tape. Rivera only appears in one scene in No Way Home , but it has become iconic for various reasons. In the scene Rivera plays Ned’s (Jacob Batalon) grandma, and then Ned and MJ (Zendaya) realize they can use Doctor Strange’s ring to create portals. It is the scene where Andrew Garfield and Tobey Maguire’s versions of Spider-Man appear for the first time in Tom Holland’s dimension, also marking their first appearance in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The appearance of the actors was famously a big secret before release of the film and fans across the global went wild in cinemas when they make their entrance. The scene was also notable for Filipino representation on screen, featuring two Filipino characters — Batalon is a Filipino-American born in Hawaii — including one who speaks significant parts of her dialogue in Tagalog, a first for a major Hollywood blockbuster. Rivera told Star FM Baguo that there was a “swelling in my heart,” when director Jon Watts told her she could speak in her native tongue to forcefully admonish the Spider-Men for messing up her kitchen. In an interview with Hawaii Public Radio , Rivera’s daughter Angela Kelly spoke about her mother’s role in No Way Home and what it meant to the family. “It’s been an amazing adventure. To us, she’s just my mom. But to the rest of the world, she’s Ned’s Lola,” Kelly said. “It’s humbling really, because never before in cinematic history really has there been a place for the Filipino language and culture. They did a really good job with paying attention to the details of our culture.” Rivera is survived by her husband, Alejandro Rivera; children, Carmela Jones (Jay), Paul Rivera (Leilani), Edwin Rivera, Angela Kelly (Jaime); 11 grandchildren and 4 great grandchildren. title: Serena Rossi to Receive Venice Fest’s Passion for Film Award
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 2:30am Serena Rossi Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Italian actress Serena Rossi will receive the Campari Passion for Film Award at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, organizers unveiled on Tuesday. Rossi will accept the award on Sept. 10 during a ceremony in the Sala Grande at the Palazzo del Cinema, ahead of the out-of-competition premiere of Scherzetto ( Trick ), directed by Mario Martone. Rossi stars in the film alongside Toni Servillo, Lorenzo Perrotta, Leonardo Lidi, Giovanni Ludeno and Gianluca Di Gennaro. In a statement, Rossi said returning to the Lido to receive the honor was “a true honor,” adding that passion and the search for an authentic connection with audiences had guided her career. She said presenting Scherzetto at this year’s festival alongside Martone, Servillo and the cast made the occasion “even more special.” Related Stories Movies Cabo Verde Looks Beyond the World Cup, Ivory Coast Gets Animated, Zimbabwe Has Ambition: A Chat With Locarno Open Doors Film Producers TV Disney+ Sets Release Date for Season 2 of Hit Thriller Series 'Made in Korea' The prize, presented in collaboration with the artistic direction of the Venice Film Festival , recognizes film professionals for their contribution to cinema and their creative work. Previous recipients include editor Bob Murawski, cinematographer Luca Bigazzi, composer Terence Blanchard, production designer Marcus Rowland, costume designer Arianne Phillips, production designers Tonino Zera and Paola Comencini , and director Gus Van Sant. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera said Rossi had built a career across film, television, music and voice acting, highlighting her work in a range of genres and formats. Rossi first came to prominence on Italian television with roles in series including Il Commissario Montalbano and Adriano Olivetti , before expanding into film with credits including Song ‘e Napule , Ammore e malavita , Lasciami andare and Io sono Mia , in which she portrayed singer Mia Martini. More recently, she has starred in the Rai series Mina Settembre , Netflix’s The Children’s Train and Non abbiamo bisogno di parole , and Disney’s Uonderbois . She also hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the 78th Venice Film Festival in 2021. The 83rd Venice International Film Festival runs Sept. 2-12. THR

Amazon has snatched up multiple international territories for the upcoming Baywatch reboot , picking up the hot lifeguard adventure series for much of Europe, including France, Germany, Italy, and Spain, as well as for Canada, Latin America and India, among other territories. As part of the deal, Amazon will also license the complete Baywatch back catalogue, including all nine seasons of the original Baywatch, and seasons 9 and 10 of the show, which was rebranded Baywatch Hawaii in the same territories. title: Think the Paramount-WBD Mega-Deal Has Nothing to Do With the Locarno Film Festival? Think Again!
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 4, 2026 2:00am Locarno Pro 2025 Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press The planned Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) is sure to make global waves across various parts of the film industry landscape. In fact, it already has, being the topic of debate on film studio lots, at sector players’ headquarters, in social meet-ups across the industry and, yes, also at film festivals, such as the recent Karlovy Vary fest. The 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland is also ready to take on the big issue of consolidation and its fallout, along with other hot-button sector topics, at its 2026 Locarno Pro industry program . Related Stories TV Disney+ Sets Release Date for Hit Thriller Series 'Made in Korea' Music Vicki Wickham, Influential 'Ready, Steady, Go!' Talent Booker and Producer, Dies at 87 “There are some earthquakes that are shaking up the infrastructure of the global industry,” which plays into this year’s program, Markus Duffner , director of Locarno Pro , tells THR . So, among other themes, he and his team thought: “Let’s see what happens with the merger of Paramount and Warner. Let’s see what happens with everything that AI can do, as groundbreaking technologies will change the industry.” News of the Paramount-WBD earlier this year came up as the team was in the thick of planning this year’s Locarno Pro program. “We don’t have a crystal sphere, but when we were putting together [the plans for Locarno Pro opening session] StepIn, the Paramount merger news came out,” Duffner recalls. “And we said, ‘Wow, what does it mean with all we’re talking about? But in the end, we felt it’s actually coherent with what we were already dealing with.’ So it’s not something brand new. It’s really a symptom of everything we were dealing with and discussing already.” Locarno Pro, which will once again mix educational, business and networking opportunities, runs Aug. 6-11 this year as part of the Locarno festival, which takes place in the Swiss lakeside town Aug. 5-15. “The 2026 edition of StepIn will explore how power structures, human capital, politics, AI and data-driven systems are reshaping the future of independent cinema,” Marcello Paolillo, the StepIn project manager, explains in a brochure. “The first roundtable will focus on the unprecedented pressures that independent cinema is facing today, including the influence of global streaming platforms on creative choices, the increasing use of algorithms, data and AI in decision-making, and the rapid concentration of power through mergers and industry consolidation.” After all, the Swiss festival’s industry strand is all about exploring challenges and how to address them with an eye on the future. “Locarno Pro is the platform which identifies, anticipates, and addresses the challenges faced by the European film industry, through an open space for dialogue on innovation and social impact, and through a concrete investment in the next generation,” Duffner highlights in a preview of this year’s edition on the Locarno Pro website. “Today’s talents are the leaders, producers, and filmmakers who will shape the coming era of film. This is why Locarno Pro is not a market like any other: it is the place where those who believe in cinema as an art form and a driving force for change find the tools to make it possible.” THR

title: Singapore’s First Wuxia Film ‘The House on the Moon’ Unveils Clip Ahead of Locarno Competition Bow: Director Nelson Yeo ‘Decided to Fully Embrace Genre’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 2:00am PT Singapore’s First Wuxia Film ‘The House on the Moon’ Unveils Clip Ahead of Locarno Competition Bow: Director Nelson Yeo ‘Decided to Fully Embrace Genre’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Dominates U.K. and Ireland Box Office With Massive Launch 41 minutes ago Singapore’s First Wuxia Film ‘The House on the Moon’ Unveils Clip Ahead of Locarno Competition Bow: Director Nelson Yeo ‘Decided to Fully Embrace Genre’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Raima Sen, Shrimoyee Chakraborty, Aarti Bajaj Team on Parno Mittra’s Producing Debut ‘The Music Teacher’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Momo Film Co. Singapore has never really had a wuxia feature film – though the genre was a fixture of local television in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when a wave of wuxia serials cast actors like Li Nanxing and Zhu Ming. Nelson Yeo is closing that gap with “ The House on the Moon ,” a lunar reimagining of the Chang’Er myth landing in Locarno’s international competition. Variety is exclusively unveiling a clip from the film, ahead of its world premiere. Related Stories Margot Robbie, Mark Ruffalo, Daisy Ridley, Omar Sy Projects Lead Venice Immersive Lineup 'Matchbox' Trailer: John Cena Stars in Toy Car Action Movie From Apple TV Wuxia is the Chinese genre of sword-fighting heroes and martial fantasy that has powered everything from King Hu’s classics to Wong Kar-wai’s “Ashes of Time.” Popular on Variety “It was quite ambitious when we first started having this idea of picking wuxia,” Yeo tells Variety . “For this one I decided to fully embrace genre and see where the film can take us.” Yeo has a habit of returning to Locarno. He attended the festival’s Filmmakers Academy in 2018, then premiered his 2023 debut feature, “Dreaming & Dying,” there, where it won the Filmmakers of the Present Golden Leopard and the Swatch First Feature Award. Three years on, he’s back for a third time. “I’m super glad to be back in Locarno,” Yeo says. The film reimagines the legend of Chang’Er, the moon goddess, and her husband, the archer Hou Yi, picking up the story after Chang’Er ascends to the moon and setting her on a journey to its dark side alongside a bandit from Earth. For Yeo, the appeal was less about honoring the myth than filling in what it leaves out. “The original myth has always been so simple,” Yeo says. “As a kid, you can pretty much recite the whole story in a couple of lines and people will get it. But then at the same time, you always wonder what are these characters really going through? What are their emotions like?” He points to Peng Meng, the disciple mentioned only in passing in the traditional tale, as the character who benefited most from that expansion. “It’s just a very basic foundation,” Yeo says. “So I felt like I have more, I can take more liberties in terms of like building the character.” Even so, he adds, the story remains centered on its heroine: “Chang’Er is traveling to the dark side of the moon throughout the film, but essentially, it’s about a journey inside herself and finding herself again and finding her own voice, in fact.” That affinity for late-1980s and 1990s wuxia runs deep. Yeo grew up on Hong Kong genre cinema and the wuxia television serials that were once a fixture of Singaporean TV, and he cites Tsui Hark’s “Zu: Warriors From the Magic Mountain” as a touchstone alongside Wong Kar-wai’s “Ashes of Time.” But reviving that language now came with practical headaches. “Sourcing for the props was a nightmare,” Yeo says. “And in terms of location wise, because Singapore being such a modern city, we had a lot of trouble finding proper locations to shoot the film.” Those constraints pushed part of the production to Taiwan, Yeo’s first time filming there. “It was quite an eye opener in terms of how things are done there,” he says. The Taiwan leg also brought him into the orbit of Lee Kang-sheng , the Taiwanese thespian and longtime Tsai Ming-liang regular, a collaboration Yeo calls a highlight of the production. “He’s amazing because he’s a one-take wonder,” Yeo says. “Everything that he does on the first day is just perfect. And I’m so fortunate to work with him.” The film’s tonal balance owes much to its bandit character, written to speak Singlish and cast, Yeo says, to give audiences an entry point among a story otherwise populated by immortals. “I really wanted that character to be the one that the audience can really relate to,” he says. “After all, he a mortal in among all these immortals. He’s the closest to the audience.” The role also reshaped the film’s register. “The original character that was written was much darker and the film was much darker,” Yeo says. “I felt like having this different element, this slightly more comedic character, lightens things up a little bit.” Shot partly through virtual production, “The House on the Moon” pushed Yeo toward tools he still regards with caution. “First and foremost, I feel like virtual production is a game changer,” he says. “At the same time, it’s not so accessible to independent filmmakers because of the inherent cost of it.” He’s warier still of artificial intelligence’s growing role in production. “Nothing beats being on the real locations, having the actors interact with the space,” Yeo says. “There’s so much more room for creative freedom on set in terms of blocking or improv. Working with a cast and crew spanning Singapore, Taiwan and beyond, including a German visual effects team and an Indonesian composer based in Berlin, was, Yeo says, a deliberate widening of his usual process. As for what the film’s Locarno premiere means to him, Yeo would rather audiences approach it without a map. “I guess just to give in to their senses and not go in with any expectations,” he says. “The plot maybe on the surface it sounds really complicated, but as long as you follow the characters’ emotions, I think you’ll be fine.” Whether “The House on the Moon” spins off into a franchise remains an open question for Yeo. “If it happens, if it happens,” he says. “I won’t force it. I won’t force myself to make a sequel of the film.” He’s already looking elsewhere: a horror project he’s drafted, and “Black Sun,” a film he’s been trying to get made for more than a decade. “The House on the Moon” is produced by Tan Si En, Wendy Lie and Kuek Shee Heng for Momo Film Co (part of Fremantle), and Aview Images, in co-production with Weydemann Bros., 9LB Film, KawanKawan Media and Widewall Pictures. It is financed by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA). The film’s proof of concept secured support from the VP Innovation Fund by Singapore’s IMDA. Parallax Films holds worldwide exclusive sales rights (excluding German speaking territories, Taiwan, and Singapore) and non-exclusive rights for all other regions in Southeast Asia. The film stars Lim Shi-An, Dominick Rustam, Harry Chang and Akira Huang, with a special appearance by Lee Kang-sheng. title: Raima Sen, Shrimoyee Chakraborty, Aarti Bajaj Team on Parno Mittra’s Producing Debut ‘The Music Teacher’ (EXCLUSIVE)

The project is co-produced by Tabernacle Street Films (U.K.) and Unscripted Co (India), the production banner Mittra is launching with this film. Written and directed by Shrimoyee Chakraborty, “The Music Teacher” is her first Bengali narrative film, following her documentary “Spirit of the Wildflower” and her work as creator and presenter of “India Bites.” Chakraborty also produces for Tabernacle Street Films, alongside Mittra’s producing role for Unscripted Co. Editor Aarti Bajaj, known for her work on “Jab We Met,” “Rockstar,” “Highway,” “Tamasha,” “Sacred Games,” “Jubilee” and “Amar Singh Chamkila,” comes aboard as co-producer. Related Stories James Gunn Gave ‘Big Brother 28’ Star Rick Devens a Cameo in ‘Man of Tomorrow’ but He ‘Had to Cancel’ Margot Robbie, Mark Ruffalo, Daisy Ridley, Omar Sy Projects Lead Venice Immersive Lineup Sen takes the title role, with Niranjan Mondal, who appeared in “Laughtersane,” rounding out the cast. Popular on Variety Inspired by Chakraborty’s mother, “The Music Teacher” is set in North Kolkata and centers on a young man struggling with depression who finds a path back to life through a teacher of Rabindra Sangeet, the genre of songs composed by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore that remains central to Bengali culture. The film is billed as a tribute to Rabindra Sangeet and the educators who have preserved Bengal’s cultural heritage across generations, exploring resilience and human connection. Mittra has spent more than two decades building a career as one of Bengali cinema’s most established actors, with credits including “Doob (No Bed of Roses),” “Rajkahini,” “Apur Panchali” and “Ranjana Ami Ar Ashbona.” “‘The Music Teacher’ embodies the kind of cinema I want Unscripted Co to champion – stories that are deeply rooted, emotionally resonant and capable of travelling across cultures,” Mittra said. “After more than two decades as an actor, producing this film marks an exciting new chapter in my creative journey. As our first production, this project represents the beginning of the vision I have for Unscripted Co, and I couldn’t have asked for a more inspiring team to bring it to life.” “‘The Music Teacher’ is my love letter to my mother, to Rabindra Sangeet and to Kolkata,” Chakraborty added. “It’s an incredibly personal story, and I’m honored to be making it alongside such an extraordinary team.” “I’ve spent my career helping shape stories in the edit room, and producing feels like a natural extension of that journey,” Bajaj said. “‘The Music Teacher’ is intimate, deeply moving and profoundly human. title: Alan Ritchson on What He Learned About Fame From Working With Arnold Schwarzenegger
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 12:55am Alan Ritchson Kierra Thorn/Getty Images Alan Ritchson took a break from his Reacher duties to star opposite Arnold Schwarzenegger in the upcoming holiday film The Man With the Bag. Directed by Adam Shankman and due to hit Amazon Prime Video on Dec. 2, the family comedy casts Schwarzenegger as Santa Claus who goes on a journey to retrieve his magic bag after its stolen. In order to get it back, he turns to his naughty list on which he finds a former thief, played by Ritchson, who comes along for the expedition. After filming with the action icon, Ritchson said he was the one who left with a valuable gift. “It was a treat,” the Reacher star told Dax Shepard and Monica Padman on a recent episode of Armchair Expert. “He taught me a lot about how gratitude should manifest in the life of somebody dealing with fame.” Related Stories TV Amanda Ip, Jay Baruchel, Ciara Bravo and Kevin Durand to Star Opposite Alan Ritchson in 'Reacher' TV Alan Ritchson Breaks Silence on Motorcycle Fight, Calls it "Scariest" Experience of His Life Ritchson said he’s transitioning to a part of his life and career where he’s aware of “how present fame is and how toxic and intrusive” it can be, not only for him but his wife, Cat, and their young boys. But he was able to watch how Schwarzenegger moved through the world and dealt with his own fans while on set and off, and that helped him shift his perspective. “I worked with Arnold, who deals with this on a degree that I will probably never experience,” he explained. “He’s dealt with it for decades on a degree that I can’t quite understand. He stops for everybody. We would be in the middle of a scene in a diner and people would be banging on the glass because our lockup wasn’t tight enough. They’re like, ‘Oh my God, will you take a picture with us?’ [He says], ‘Oh, be right there. Come outside and take a picture with us.’ He has no problem. He makes time for everybody. And so I look at that and I’m like, ‘Cat, if this is his attitude, I have no excuse.’ … He showed me something really interesting in the way that he approaches life and his lot in life. And I really deeply admire how he treats people.” Schwarzenegger and Ritchson filming a scene for Man with the Bag in New York on Jan. 15, 2025. Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images/Getty Images THR

title: Haugesund New Nordic Films Unveils French Focus Including a Case Study on ‘Ibelin,’ From ‘The Imitation Game’ Director Morten Tyldum (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 12:45am PT Haugesund New Nordic Films Unveils French Focus Including a Case Study on ‘Ibelin,’ From ‘The Imitation Game’ Director Morten Tyldum (EXCLUSIVE) French prodco Les Valseurs will pitch two out of four French projects selected for the Nordic Co-Production Market By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest Erik Poppe’s ‘Beloved’ to Open Haugesund: ‘All Eyes Are on Norway,’ Says Festival Chief Tonje Hardersen 1 day ago DR Sales Closes With WDR/Arte, VRT, NRK in Multi Buyers Pact on Norwegian Wildlife Doc ‘Frost Without Snow and Ice’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago U.K. Heavyweight Doc Player Jane Ray Boards Argentina’s ‘The Nights’ by Ana Bovino Ahead of ECAM Forum (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago See All 'All the Softness in the World' Courtesy of Les Valseurs New Nordic Films , the Norwegian International Film Festival’s industry confab in Haugesund, has announced the program for its first ever French Focus, set up to foster partnerships and co-productions between France and the Nordic countries. The event, due to run Aug. 25-28, is organised by New Nordic Films in partnership with the Institut Francais de Norvège, the French Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs, France’s National Center for Cinema ( CNC ) and promotional body Unifrance . Related Stories Margot Robbie, Mark Ruffalo, Daisy Ridley, Omar Sy Projects Lead Venice Immersive Lineup 'Matchbox' Trailer: John Cena Stars in Toy Car Action Movie From Apple TV Headlining the French Focus is a pitching session on Aug. 26 at the Nordic Co-Production Market of four French films in development, of which two are produced by pedigreed producer Les Valseurs , a Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner this year for “ Elephants in the Fog ” and Un Certain Regard top prize winner in 2025 for “ The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo .” Produced by Les Valseurs co-founder Damien Megherdi, “Borderline” is the feature length spin-off of Yves Piat ’s Oscar and César nominated short film “Nefta Football Club,” while “All the Softness in the World” is an ambitious animation project by Turkish artist Ayçe Kartal whose short film “Wicked Girl” was the first animation short to scoop the Grand Prix in Clermont-Ferrand in 2018. Popular on Variety Two other directorial debuts make the cut: the creative documentary “Boutès” by Jeanne Géli and Loïs Szymczak, produced by Womanray’s Marielle Tricoire, co-producer of Jim Jarmusch’s “Father Mother Sister Brother” and “Temporary Lives” by Syrian-Norwegian filmmaker Wessam Hachicho, produced by Respiro Productions (“In the Nguyen Kitchen”). Besides the four-title pitch, the French Focus will include a panel on co-production opportunities between France and the five Nordic countries, and a case study on the anticipated “ Ibelin ” by Norwegian-born Morten Tyldum, mostly famed for the Oscar-winning “The Imitation Game.” The biopic about online gamer Mats Steen – starring Charlie Plummer, Stephen Graham, Toni Collette, and Bill Nighy – is currently in production for France’s Vendôme Pictures, Pathé, and Norway’s Neby-Tyldum AS. “I am incredibly happy that we are finally able to have a French focus in Haugesund,” said Gyda Velvin Myklebust, head of New Nordic Films. “French cinema is well-known internationally for high artistic quality, and we in the Nordic region have also recently made a strong mark internationally,” she added, referring to “Sentimental Value”’s Oscar win for Best International Feature, the first ever for Norway. “France and the Nordics have highly talented and ambitious filmmakers, and we believe our French focus will give wind to a French-Nordic wave of co-productions and creative collaborations between our countries.” For Kjersti Mo , CEO at the Norwegian Film Institute (NFI) the French Focus reflects “a growing recognition that European film depends on stronger international collaboration.” “France has one of Europe’s strongest film cultures and most developed production ecosystems, while the Nordic countries bring distinctive stories, strong creative talent and considerable international experience,” Mo added. “These different strengths are precisely what can make the partnerships valuable,” said the NFI chief, who also underscored that “international collaboration is a central priority” in the institute’s new strategy. Speaking to Variety, Michel Plazanet, CNC director of international affairs, pointed out that “the Nordic countries, which traditionally co-produce extensively among themselves, are now “seeking additional partners, particularly in France, as this opens up numerous opportunities: access to funding (such as “Aide aux Cinémas du Monde,” regional co-production funds, Arte, and SOFICA), distribution advantages (French sales agents have an excellent reputation, and French co-productions gain easier access to the Cannes and Annecy festivals), and better access to the French theatrical market, the largest in Europe, especially for arthouse cinema.” Conversely the Nordics offer clear advantages for French producers, Plazanet said, as the region boasts “robust institutions, substantial and diverse public and private funding, and reliable professionals accustomed to international co-production.” Aide au Cinéma du Monde So far 20 Nordic projects have received backing from the ACM including three Cannes entries from Joachim Trier (“Sentimental Value,” “The Worst Person in the World,” “Louder than Bombs”), and two from Tarik Saleh (“Eagles of the Republic,” Boys from Heaven”). Denmark, Norway, and Sweden are the most active [co-production] countries, but Iceland also performs very well, given its very small population,” Plazanet said. Among the French Focus attendees, Julie Billy, founder of Paris-based June Films, was just granted ACM support for the Icelandic project in production “A Favour” by Grímur Hákonarson (“Rams”), and is developing a project with Norway’s Eye Eye Pictures (“Fjord,” “Sentimental Value”). “The French Focus comes at exactly the right moment,” said the producer, also interested in creators – notably from the Sámi community, “whose perspectives are unique and increasingly important on the international scene.” “I would love to see Norway as a minority co-producer in more French productions, and of course the other way around,” added Eye Eye Pictures co-founder Andrea Berendsen Ottmar who also hopes the French Focus will “inspire, so that we can help each other to think outside the box in terms of how we structure and finance our projects. Independent producers all over Europe need to stand together and support each other, and forums like this are very valuable in that sense,” she observed. As noted by Plazanet, the French Focus plays within a series of French/Nordic industry events, multiplied in the last two years, that peaked in 2025 with the Visions Nordiques Festival in Paris. Next on the CNC’s top agenda is “an institutional alignment on key European issues, notably the transposition of the AVMS Directive and platform obligations.” The Norwegian International Film festival, running Aug. 22-28, will platform eight French films in its section French Touch. Drilling down on the four French projects lined-up for the Nordic Co-Production Market “Bordeline” (“Sur la ligne,” Yves Piat) Produced by Daniel Megherbi, Les Valseurs Feature debut from the director of the 2020 Oscar-nominated short film “Neftah Football Club who has sketched out ideas from his short, together with writer Alaa Eddine Aljem (“The Unknown Saint”). The story turns Hishem, on a customs officer on the Algerian-Tunisian border, who encounters Tesla, a donkey lost in the desert with headphones over his ears, with a bag of cocaine on his back. Producer Megherbi who co-produced with the Nordics Nepalese pic “Elephants in the Fog,” a Cannes’ Jury Prize winner, believes “Bordeline”’s deadpan, absurd humor, “somewhere between Elia Suleiman and the Coen brothers,” will resonate well with Nordic partners and the general audience. Public backers on board include the CNC, Région Nouvelle-Aquitaine and ICEC in Spain via Spanish co-producers Sumendi and BTeam Pictures. Filming is pencilled for April-May 2027. “All the Softness in the World” (“Toute la douceur du monde,” Ayçe Kartal) Produced by Damien Megherbi, Les Valseurs Turkish animation filmmaker Ayçe Kartal and Megherbi reunite on the helmer’s feature length debut after his multi-awarded short film “Wicked Girls,” an Annecy Jury Prize) winner. Set in 1950, the story follows the young Levon who has grown up posing as a girl, to be protected from an ancient family vendetta. In his search for his true identity, Levon lands in Paris in the world of Haute Couture where he begins to recover a sense of self through creativity. “I want to explore, through [Levon] an alternative history of fashion, one rooted in survival, not spectacle,” said Kartal in a statement. “At Haugesund, we hope to find a Nordic co-producer who understands what we’re trying to achieve with this project. It’s an ambitious, innovative piece of adult animation, and we want a partner who’s genuinely excited by that,” said Megherbi who’s secured development support from the CNC and Hauts-de-France region. “Boutès” (Jeanne Géli, Loïs Szymczak) Produced by Marieke Tricoire, Womanray A liife-affirming documentary in which forensic pathologist Jeanne Géli turns filmmaker to capture the frailty and beauty of life, as her partner Loic Szymczak, an Olympic diver and visual artist, suddenly fights for his own life, upended by a malignant brain tumor. Together they move towards one act of faith-a performative dive in the heart of Paris. “This film is, above all, a love story. We are making it to transform the reality of illness into poetic material,” said the co-directors. Womanray founder Tricoire, who bridges luxury brands with film and served as co-producer on Jim Jarmusch’s Golden Lion winner “Father, Mother, Sister, Brother,” said she signed up for New Nordic Films when she found out that the founder of the extreme sport Døds diving (Death diving) was born in Norway. The project co-produced with Hutong in France, is currently shooting, with a delivery pencilled for 2028. “Temporary Lives” (Wessam Hachicho) Produced by Amélie Quéret, Respiro Productions Wessam Hachicho, a graduate from Oslo’s Westerdals film school and a former cinematographer in Syria, draws from her own uprooting experience to tell the story of a Syrian teenager refugee in Oslo and his estranged father as they seek asylum in Norway. “Beneath the [film’s] political context lies an intimate story about unresolved trauma, family bonds and the sacrifices parents and children make for one another,” said Hachicho. The film also asks how institutions shape individual lives, as every decision the characters make becomes a negotiation between survival, dignity, and hope.” Queret, who met the rising filmmaker at the Less is More Lab, said she was blown away by Hachicho’s script and “clear artistic identity.” In Haugesund, she will be looking for a Norwegian co-producer and access to Nordic funds. Filming is due to start in 2027. title: Hwang Bo-reum, Lee Geum-yi Among Authors in Busan Story Market’s 2026 Selections
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 12:33am PT Hwang Bo-reum, Lee Geum-yi Among Authors in Busan Story Market’s 2026 Selections By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Dominates U.K. and Ireland Box Office With Massive Launch 41 minutes ago Singapore’s First Wuxia Film ‘The House on the Moon’ Unveils Clip Ahead of Locarno Competition Bow: Director Nelson Yeo ‘Decided to Fully Embrace Genre’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Raima Sen, Shrimoyee Chakraborty, Aarti Bajaj Team on Parno Mittra’s Producing Debut ‘The Music Teacher’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Photo by Sasha Don The Busan Story Market (BSM) has unveiled 25 official selections for 2026, including international bestseller Hwang Bo-reum and two-time Hans Christian Andersen Award finalist Lee Geum-yi, drawing on original IP from four Asian countries. BSM is part of the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the official market of the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF). Among the Korean selections is “My Upstairs Neighbors” by Hwang Bo-reum, the author behind the international bestseller “Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop,” and “Chasm of Sorrow” by Lee Geum-yi, whose more than 50 published books and international translations have made her one of Korea’s most recognized children’s and young-adult authors. The lineup as a whole comprises 15 titles from Korea and four each from Taiwan and Japan, alongside two from Indonesia. Related Stories 'Matchbox' Trailer: John Cena Stars in Toy Car Action Movie From Apple TV Margot Robbie, Mark Ruffalo, Daisy Ridley, Omar Sy Projects Lead Venice Immersive Lineup Genres and narratives range widely this year, spanning stories that explore universal emotions and relationships, including life and death, family, growth, love and loss, through fresh genre settings, alongside plot-driven works built around hidden agendas and fixations that take unpredictable turns. Popular on Variety BSM operates as a marketplace connecting film and audiovisual adaptations of original IP, drawing from books, webtoons, web novels, video games and other formats, with content platforms and IP holders worldwide. The official selections take part in pitching sessions and one-on-one business meetings aimed at secondary rights deals and adaptation collaborations. For the Korean IP selection, BSM fielded 138 submissions from 83 companies this year, ultimately choosing 15 titles from 13 companies: nine books, two webtoons, two web novels and two stories. Books make up more than half the Korean lineup, though the selections stay broadly balanced across formats and genres. The titles pair crowd-pleasing categories, among them romance, mystery, fantasy and family drama, with less conventional hooks, including parallel worlds, out-of-body experiences and science fiction, touching on themes from generational communication and family bonds to individual lives set against their times. The selection ranges from emotionally driven human dramas to AI-inflected fantasy, genre-blending historical romance, period pieces and hybrid concepts. BSM’s Taiwanese IP selection, conducted annually with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), yielded four titles from four companies, one apiece drawn from books, webtoons, web novels and comics. Each centers on a high concept distinctive enough to convey its identity in a single line, using fantasy settings not merely for spectacle but to work through emotional terrain that includes bereavement, remorse, early romance, ties between family members and coming of age, positioning the titles for adaptation across film, drama series and other formats. Four Japanese IPs from four companies, one book and three comics, were chosen through the Visual Industry Promotion Organization (VIPO). The selections lean on layered characters and relationships built around secrets and obsessions, with stories shifting in unpredictable directions as hidden truths surface or unlikely individuals form bonds across boundaries. Indonesia’s two selections, both comics from two separate companies, were picked from a shortlist of 10 Indonesian original IPs that had been presented at the 2025 JAFF Content Market, an initiative run by the Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival Market (JAFF Market); the pair emerged after a round of pitches and meetings centered on adapting the properties for film and audiovisual formats. Both took home the JAFF Content Market Award Goes to ACFM 2026, earning them a spot in this year’s BSM lineup. JAFF Content Market has since evolved into JAFF IP Connection for 2026, and one of BSM’s selected Korean IPs will be invited to that program following talks with JAFF Market representatives. The Yogyakarta, Indonesia program runs Nov. 28-30, continuing the two-way exchange of original IP between BSM and JAFF Market. BSM runs alongside APM at ACFM, which takes over Exhibition Center 2 at BEXCO in Busan for four days starting Oct. 10, with the 25 selections set to connect with industry professionals through BSM Pitch & Match sessions and further business meetings exploring IP expansion and adaptation opportunities. ACFM is the official market of BIFF and is held in Busan every October. The 2025 edition, ACFM’s 20th, drew industry professionals from 55 countries – 3,024 of them, alongside 1,222 registered companies – with on-site attendance reaching a record 30,006. The Sales Market tallied 8,438 business meetings, generating an estimated $71.1 million in transactions. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15, with the 21st ACFM held Oct. 10-13. title: Cabo Verde Looks Beyond the World Cup, Ivory Coast Gets Animated, Zimbabwe Has Ambition: A Chat With Locarno Open Doors Film Producers
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 4, 2026 12:01am Locarno Open Doors Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors Open Doors , the Locarno Film Festival ‘s co-production platform and talent development program for filmmakers from equity-seeking communities and regions where artistic expression is at risk, is ready for its 2026 edition . It is its second that is putting a spotlight on African cinema . The Open Doors Producers program supports producers in their efforts to build sustainable careers and cross-border networks, bringing to the Swiss city six participants. They are Tapiwa Chipfupa of Ambidextrous Pictures in Zimbabwe, an EAVE alumn who recently launched the international training and mentorship program Audiovisual Entrepreneurs Laboratory (AVEL); Adja Mariam Mahre Soro from the Ivory Coast, or Côte d’Ivoire, who leads Studio Kä, an animation studio she founded in Abidjan; Natasha Craveiro from Cabo Verde, whose company Korikaxoru Films produced Omi Nobu , which featured in the Open Doors Screenings at Locarno 2025; veteran Mamounata Nikiema of Pilumpiku Production in Burkina Faso; Nigerian producer David Ikeata of Vox Cinematic Films; and Rua Osman from Sudan, whose Helomur Picture has been behind such festival favorites as Goodbye Julia (Cannes, 2023). Related Stories TV Disney+ Sets Release Date for Season 2 of Hit Thriller Series 'Made in Korea' Music Phil Collins Reveals He Nearly Died During 2024 Hospitalization After Years of Alcohol Abuse Yanis Gaye, a French-Senegalese creative producer, co-founder of the boutique production houses Goree Cinema in Senegal and Strange Fruit Production House in France, also co-founded Yetu (Un)Limited, a multi-venture African film studio. At Locarno, he serves as head of studies at Open Doors. And he connected THR with some of the producers attending this year’s edition. “It’s interesting because you see a lot of territories represented that you would think have a lot of challenges in terms of infrastructure and local industry itself,” he explained about the Open Door 2026 participants. “But this is where you actually see the resilience and the most innovative models. Because you have to be bold in a way that allows you not just to produce content, but also to shape your own ecosystem.” Continued Gaye: “The nature or the profile of the African producer is much closer to an entrepreneur and social entrepreneur. … It’s about working on multiple things at the same time, so usually those producers and their companies tackle many verticals at the same time.” Running Aug. 5-10, the Open Doors program offers hands-on training, mentoring and networking, along with public screenings and events during the Locarno Film Festival and its industry arm Locarno Pro . Before they all dive into a busy week in Switzerland, THR talked to Soro from the Ivory Coast, Zimbabwe’s Chipfupa and Craveiro from Cabo Verde about what projects they are currently working on and what they expect from the Open Doors experience in Locarno. What’s your hope for the Open Doors experience? NATASHA CRAVEIRO I am really, really happy that I will get this opportunity to be in Locarno to meet people, to be in this program that is so very well designed, and they are so attentive to our needs. My expectation is to meet people with whom we can collaborate and who get to know Cape Verde from another point of view that is not the football [FIFA World Cup] point of view. Not that it’s not a good opportunity. People still have the name [of our country] in their heads. It’s a good opportunity to say, yes, we have football, but we do have cinema too. TAPIWA CHIPFUPA Like Natasha, I am extremely excited. The online program has been really awesome for me already. It has been curated for me or around me. So, I already have so much that I’ve learned. I’ve gotten to know the other producers a little bit, so I’m really excited to actually see them face-to-face and to have more discussions. The program they’ve outlined to us for Locarno looks so exciting. I feel that if we apply ourselves, we’ll be able to develop it into something so much bigger. So, I’m feeling really privileged. Tapiwa Chipfupa of Ambidextrous Pictures in Zimbabwe Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors ADJA MARIAM MAHRE SORO I’m also very happy to be part of this program and to be selected. We do animation, which is not necessarily the kind of work and projects for which they used to have producers in Open Doors. I was curious to see how our reality can fit with the program, and online, it was already very, very interesting. So I look [forwward to] Locarno and will just follow the flow, meet new people, make good experiences and enjoy the moments. Are you bringing specific projects to Locarno? SORO I am coming with a young adult animated series. That is not something that we used to have coming from Africa for a global audience, with taekwondo and murder and many things in it. So I’m curious to see how the the producers at Locarno who focus more on feature films see this kind of opportunity. CRAVEIRO I’m also coming with projects, two hybrid features. And I am looking, of course, for financing, for co-producers. Both are talking a lot about our reality in Cape Verde. One is more related to environmental protection and the worries we have now that we are seeing tourism exploding. We are getting more worried every day. And of course, we are happy for the World Cup, but it’s an extra worry for us because we know we are not even prepared for the numbers of tourism we have already. The other project is about the post-colonial Cape Verde. It’s a country that doesn’t talk about the colonial traumas. And that is sticking with us generation after generation, 50 years after our independence [in 1975 from Portuguese colonial rule]. Natasha Craveiro of Korikaxoru Films in Cabo Verde Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors CHIPFUPA I’m coming with a supernatural thriller based in a village. It’s about a young girl who defies the patriarchy and tradition to ultimately become the unlikely savior of the village. I am obviously looking for financing partners, people who are interested in developing a short as a proof of concept. But I’m also in the process of trying to contribute to the local ecosystem here in Zimbabwe, as our industry is still really developing. I’ve been developing some initiatives for which I would really love to find people to partner with. The first one is a producers’ lab that is already supported by Berlinale Talents, and I am looking for ways to continue that and keep that alive. And recently, I started an initiative for young women and girl creatives in the film and art sector. Locarno is an opportunity not just to showcase our films, but to look at how else we can help or we can contribute to the development of the continental sector as well. CRAVEIRO We do have these kind of projects too because we are also still struggling to build a healthy ecosystem. We have the Cine Club project because we feel that the audience needs to be educated, and you have to go get them. We have so we have the Cinet Club. Our company also has this academy through which we try to help young people who have an idea to transform it into a project. And we do have this festival that we started last year. So, I’m also looking for partners who are interested and who can help us to take these steps, these baby steps that we need to take. Adja Mariam Mahre Soro of Studio Kä in Ivory Coast Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors SORO In Côte d’Ivoire, until last year, it was a real challenge. There was a real gap between what we know about animation and what our government knew about animation. They had to understand that we need to build an ecosystem to have talents who know how to make animation, we need to have schools, we need to have a real ecosystem. But now they have started to understand it. For example, I have the chance to collaborate with the Ministry of Communication on an animation school pilot for 25 young animators and see how that can be a way to improve our schools that already exist and their curriculum. Last year, we also signed a treaty of co-production with Belgium, and we are also having a conversation with Canada. So there is movement now. We also have an event in November where we invite Japan in Côte d’Ivoire to talk about animation, so there is a real desire to do something in Côte d’Ivoire. THR

title: Ariana Grande Wants to “Clear the Air” About Upcoming Break From Public Eye: “Not a Reactive or Impulsive Thing”

title: ‘Ice Cream Man’ Review: Eli Roth’s Small-Town Horror Flick Is for Diehard Slasher Fans, and Absolutely No One Else
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All August 3, 2026 8:00pm Ari Millen in 'Ice Cream Man.' Valerie Flores/The Horror Section If you’re looking up the credits for Ice Cream Man on IMDB, you might as well skip past director/co-screenwriter Eli Roth and the extensive cast list. Because the real stars of this ultra-gonzo horror film are the folks in the makeup department, especially prosthetics designers Steve Newburn and Adrien Morot (the latter an Oscar winner for his work on The Whale ). Sure, Roth came up with the story and co-wrote the screenplay. But his efforts would have been for naught if you didn’t fully believe the sights of young children dismembering their parents’ bodies or playing games of tetherball and tag with human heads. Not to mention the tug of war using human intestines. Related Stories Business 'Terrifier' Actress Had Deal for 1 Percent of Profits. A Court Will Decide If That's for One Movie -- Or the Whole Series Movies 'Hershey' Biopic Trailer: Finn Wittrock, Alexandra Daddario Struggle to Make Affordable Chocolate If all of that sounds like a euphoric cinematic experience, then this the film for you. It’s certainly the film for its auteur, who conceived the idea more than two decades ago and has been trying to make it ever since. Since the major studios passed on his idea about a townful of kids turned into crazed, murderous zombies, Roth formed his own company, The Horror Section, to distribute his labor of love. Not surprisingly, the film is being released unrated. Ice Cream Man The Bottom Line Catnip for gorehounds. Release date : Friday, August 7 Cast : Ari Millen, Benjamin Byron Davis, Eli Roth, Karen Cliche, Dylan Hawco, Sarah Abbott, Shiloh O’Reilly, Kiori Mirza Waldman, Charlie Zeltzer, Charlie Storey Director : Eli Roth Screenwriters : Eli Roth, Noah Benson 1 hour 26 minutes The film doesn’t feature a particularly complicated scenario. The strange-looking driver of a weirdly decorated ice cream truck driving through the sort of idyllic American small town painted by Norman Rockwell distributes his frozen wares to the local children, and they promptly turn into homicidal little creatures staring blankly into space and sporting severely discolored lips. They go after their adult prey with such demonic enthusiasm it makes you wonder why George Romero never thought of the idea, a sort of “Bugsy Malone of the Living Dead.” One hopes Roth has gotten his worst instincts out with this effort, which, considering that it comes from the maker of such films as Cabin Fever , Hostel and Thanksgiving , is saying something. The silent, perpetually smiling ice cream truck vendor, played chillingly by Canadian actor Ari Millen ( Orphan Black ), is certainly a creepy figure who could give Art the Clown in the Terrifier movies a run for his money. Except that the Ice Cream Man is less a psycho killer than an evil enabler, one whose frozen treats turn otherwise normal children into pint-sized killing machines displaying remarkable ingenuity in their methods of slaughter. The Ice Cream Man does pitch in at times, including serving a teacher’s scooped-out brains to him in a cone. The little darlings, who include a girl who walks around the neighborhood holding her mother’s severed head like a trophy, display the usual playfulness of summer campers. They also seek to swell their ranks by force-feeding the ice cream to any fellow children who haven’t yet been infected. Their carnage — exemplified in a lengthy, virtuosic sequence in which they attack the adult teachers and employees at their grade school with frenzied abandon — includes the sort of gruesome playground activities involving severed body parts that makes one hope the child actors had recourse to on-set psychiatric counseling. There’s a backstory of sorts, told by a local priest (Benjamin Byron Davis) and involving a travesty of justice followed by revenge facilitated by a necromancer. But it almost seems unnecessary, since the film’s true raison d’etre is demonstrating the amazing talents of its prosthetics designers, who have created such a relentless series of horrific bodily images that it’s easy to imagine blood-crazed audiences applauding them like musical numbers. The reliance on practical effects rather than the CGI employed by so many current horror films at least proves refreshing. The visuals are also packed with throwaway jokes, including one drive-by decapitation that should be accompanied by a rim shot, and deadpan visual flourishes like a crow pecking out the eyes of a corpse in the foreground of a shot. There have been plenty of horror movies involving murderous children over the years, such as Village of the Damned and its sequel and, of course, Children of the Corn . But Roth doesn’t hide his desire to outdo them all with this effort that can only be described as sick and twisted. And I’m sure he’ll take that as a compliment.
