title: ‘Ice Cream Man’ Review: Eli Roth Blends ‘Home Alone’ And ‘Hostel’ For Over-The-Top Unrated Bloodfest
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Late Fame’ Review: Willem Dafoe And Greta Lee Superb In Wonderful Indie Film About Art And Rediscovery In A New York Long Gone ‘Ice Cream Man’ Review: Eli Roth Blends ‘Home Alone’ And ‘Hostel’ In Over The Top Unrated Bloodfest In Search Of A Story ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Review: Tom Holland And Zendaya Forge A Challenging Path Forward In Dark And Thrilling New Chapter From Marvel Superhero, Spider-Man View All August 3, 2026 8:00pm Ice Cream Man The Horror Section Taking a cue from the likes of Jason, Freddy, Leatherface, Michael Myers, Chucky, Candyman, and countless others, Horrormeister Eli Roth has now realized a 20 year dream to give the same fame in the genre to the Ice Cream Man in the simply titled new film, Ice Cream Man. That’s right. Roth hopes to immortalize the guy who drives around neighborhoods in that musical ice cream truck, the one kids have flocked to ever since wheels were invented. What he has created is just another excuse for mind-numbing graphic terror, but unfortunately has forgotten to provide much of a plot to keep us hooked. The filmmaker felt no studio would touch his vision of unfiltered gross-out dismemberings and the movie is being released unrated and under the moniker of The Horror Section, a new distributor Roth has created to put it into theatres. Related Stories News 'Ice Cream Man' Review: Eli Roth Blends 'Home Alone' And 'Hostel' In Over The Top Unrated Bloodfest In Search Of A Story Documentary 'Death Boom' Review: Eli Roth & Leonardo DiCaprio Among Producers Of Docu Warning Baby Boomers To Be Ready: The End Is Coming, And It Is Not Pretty - Tribeca Festival Essentially the director is taking the idea of seeing kids unleashed to invoke whatever pain they can possibly muster on adults ala Home Alone but making it so gross-out bloodletting that it would get an NC 17 if a rating were slapped on it. What Roth, and his longtime screenwriting partner Noah Belson have concocted is an unfleshed-out idea that is just left with the flesh. Watch on Deadline Opening on a typical sunny summer day in a fictional American small town called Bayleen Bay, we see a little league game in progress when an Ice Cream truck comes rolling in and the propreitor, a man with a creepy smile begins handing out free samples to all the kids. What a nice gesture. Uh, not. The ice cream man has revenge on his mind because as we will later discover via flashbacks, he was bullied and battered years earlier by the other kids in the town, leading to a miserable life. Now he is back, those kids are now the parents of a new generation that unknowingly is being weaponized thru his ice cream in order to have them kill their parents and everyone else over the age of 12. This is a man serving up double scoops of terror but the children are doing his bidding while he approvingly looks on. When these kids march into the school the next day like zombies with colorful flavors of ice cream smeared across their mouths, the grown ups do not know what they are in for but about 15 minutes into what appeared to be just a nice idyllic film, all hell breaks loose and these kids one by one start chainsawing off heads, some unmentionable parts, legs, arms, hands , feet – you name it. They find new inventive uses for daddy’s power tools, make jumpropes out of guts, serve up scoops of the school principal’s brains, and well, you get the picture. Chopping up their parents and teachers has never been so much fun as these kids take command gleefully and with joy as the ice cream man (actor Ari Millen in a dialogue-less performance) leads the band. If all this sounds like your kind of entertainment, I suggest you check in with your therapist. Roth is pretty gleeful himself, a director who has taken the genre to the limits in movies like 2002’s Cabin Fever, 2005’s torture porn Hostel , and the 2023 holiday horror flick Thanksgiving which was the feature film realization of a ludicrous fake theatrical trailer in Quentin Tarantino’s Grindhouse, but here he is really stretching the limits of taste, no doubt intentionally. Unfortunately the timing is off as this underdeveloped concept looks like a bad attempted imitation of last summer’s far superior Zach Cregger directed smash hit Oscar winning Weapons which had a similar idea of a whole town’s kids being mysteriously weaponized. Ice Cream Man feels like a (very) low budget attempt to capitalize and exploit, even if Roth has waited 20 years to get it made. Also it seems ill-timed since this year has also seen smart reinventions of the horror genre with the likes of Obsession and Backrooms finding critical acclaim and huge audiences. With this film though we are just back to basics with no ambition beyond finding ways to tear the human body apart that somehow we haven’t seen before. There is even one kid carrying around his severed mother’s head like a stuffed teddy bear. Sweet. Now it does appear Roth and company are going for laughs in some ways, the absurdity of it all, and I must confess it works in one scene with a priest hiding from the ice cream man and delivering complex instructions to three kids who have thus far avoided the curse so they can break the spell and end this holy terror: “You kill the siren, you cut the Necromancer’s head off, he’ll be wearing a ceremonial cloak, but do not remove the hood, find the ice cream man and remove the hood, make the ice cream man look into the Necromancer’s eyes, that will kill him”. Got all that? No spoiler alert on if the kids succeed in this daunting task, but it does all end with a spirited rap tune written and sung by none other than Snoop Dogg. “I Scream. You Scream. We Scream. ICE CREAM!” Producers are Roth and Kate Harrison Karman. She will play the role of Sandra, we hear. HBO Max and DCS declined to comment for this story. Season 1 will be centered around DC bad guy Gorilla Grodd, who has psychic powers and other skills after his encounter with an alien spaceship. title: ‘Late Fame’ Review:  Willem Dafoe And Greta Lee Superb In Wonderful Indie Film About Art And Rediscovery In A New York Long Gone
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Late Fame’ Review: Willem Dafoe And Greta Lee Superb In Wonderful Indie Film About Art And Rediscovery In A New York Long Gone ‘Ice Cream Man’ Review: Eli Roth Blends ‘Home Alone’ And ‘Hostel’ In Over The Top Unrated Bloodfest In Search Of A Story ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Review: Tom Holland And Zendaya Forge A Challenging Path Forward In Dark And Thrilling New Chapter From Marvel Superhero, Spider-Man View All August 3, 2026 4:59pm Late Fame Killer Films Late Fame , which premiered a year ago this month at the Venice Film Festival, is a gem. It is a movie about, among other things, discovery and rediscovery. It may be a year after critics first saw this movie that I am only just discovering now as it begins its theatrical engagements, but if ever there was a beguiling and enlightening film hiding in plain sight, it is this one from director Kent Jones ( Diane) and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Samy Burch ( May December). Related Stories News 45 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026 News The 63 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office Based on Arthur Schnitzler’s 1890’s novella, Burch has modernized it and changed the Vienna setting to New York City’s Soho district, a once-bustling enclave for artists and poets and now something quite different. Ed Saxberger ( Willem Dafoe ) has worked for the post office for 37 years, but in the late ’70s he was a published poet with a brief dance with notoriety, a couple of articles written about his modest paperback, now relegated to the back shelves of a dusty private bookstore, if you can even find it there. Meyers ( Edmund Donovan ), the leader of a young group of men with respect for those who came before and whose little salon competes with “influencers” tied to their iPhones in the same space, indeed has discovered Saxberger and intends to make him the group’s next project, an excavation of greatness somehow passed over but ripe for renewal. Setting out to find Saxberger, he encounters this modest man whose current social interactions are with blue-collar colleagues at the local bar and a peaceful existence in his humble apartment. Friends only know Ed as a fellow postal worker, certainly not as a man who once wrote poems with the gift of Frost. But that was another life, another time, and so when Meyers invites Ed to his group it is met with some resistance. He can’t even fathom how this guy even could find his book, much less want to praise it. Watch on Deadline Nevertheless he shows up, and thus begins his relationship with the self-called Enthusiasm Society, a gathering of twentysomething admirers, if not much else, who call themselves intellectuals and reject technology in favor of art and poetry. Indeed their recognition of him as a kind of genius eventually wins over Ed, who begins to remember the love for creativity that once drove his life in a very different era, a lost New York where art was prized. And there also is Gloria ( Greta Lee ), the older female friend of the Enthusiasm Society, an actress and singer and somewhat tragic if flamboyant personality whom they also have latched on to. Ed finds something in common with her, even if they are the exact opposites in demeanor. By her very nature she begins to light up his life, especially when she agrees to perform his poetry at a show the Society is going to produce, one advertising new poetry from this lost genius. What makes this film work as well as it does, even if inspired by material from well over a century ago, is first and foremost a truly splendid cast. Dafoe continues to be a miracle of an actor, never overplaying his hand here and believably embodying a man resigned to a different life than what might have been — a richly talented writer of long ago suddenly reawakened after putting it all in the past. His skepticism is real and so is his awareness that these newfound admirers may not see him for who he really is and what his poetry is really about. Lee, so fine in a wide variety of roles from Past Lives to The Morning Show , is superb as a woman playing a role in life as well as piano bars. Fortunately she is no stereotype here as Gloria is a genuine talent herself, an exceptional performer as she proves singing Brecht and Weill’s “Surabaya Johnny” in a beautiful moment with Ed in the audience recognizing he is also seeing someone deserving of late fame herself. Unfortunately she has demons, and Lee is truly stunning in a role that runs the gamut. Donovan is perfect as the leader of a group who essentially adopts artists for their own sense of worth. Burch’s brilliantly witty, biting and all-knowing screenplay never satirizes these characters or looks down on them in a movie Jones and his exceptional actors have blessed with sheer humanity and grace. Producers are Pamela Koffler, Christine Vachon, Mason Plotts, Danny Roberts H.S. Naji, Jackie Langelier, Taylor Shung and Ethan Lazar.
